text: SOX isn't a privacy law, it's a financial-reporting law. But the infrastructure it demands, access controls, segregation of duties, audit trails, is exactly what data governance builds. This lesson covers SOX and three sector-specific rules you'll hear named constantly.

Sarbanes-Oxley was enacted in 2002, after a wave of accounting scandals, Enron and WorldCom chief among them. It applies to publicly traded companies and their auditors, and it exists to make sure a public company's financial reports are accurate and that the controls behind them can be trusted.

Two sections matter most. Section 302 requires corporate officers, typically the CEO and CFO, to personally certify the accuracy of financial reports, which only works if the underlying data is actually correct. Section 404 requires management to assess internal controls over financial reporting, and requires an independent auditor to attest to that assessment. In practice, that means tracking who can change financial data, whether changes are logged, and whether duties are properly separated.

SOX also created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, adding independent, external scrutiny on top of a company's own controls. And beyond SOX, three sector-specific rules come up constantly: PCI DSS for payment card data, GLBA for financial-services customer information, and FERPA for student education records. Each one governs a specific category of data wherever it applies, on top of whatever general privacy law also applies.

You don't need to master any of these in depth, just recognize the pattern: a named rule exists for payment cards, financial-services data, and student records. Next up: privacy by design, where protection gets built in from the start instead of bolted on.
